lead: Every 3D scene has surfaces behind surfaces. Hidden surface removal decides which surface the eye sees at each pixel. The Z-buffer works in image space: it keeps one depth value per pixel beside the colour, and a new fragment replaces the old only if it is nearer. A BSP tree works in object space: polygon planes split space into front and back, so polygons are drawn back to front. Games, CAD viewers and map renderers use both.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for plane equations and face normals; Unit 2 for projection to screen coordinates.

blocks.text: An object-space method decides visibility from polygon geometry. The painter's algorithm sorts polygons by distance and draws far to near, so near paint covers far paint. It is cheap but fails when three polygons overlap cyclically, because no single order is correct.

The Z-buffer is an image-space method. It stores a colour buffer and a depth buffer with one depth per pixel. If smaller z means nearer, initialise every depth to the far value z_far. Rasterise each polygon. At each pixel, compare the polygon's depth z with the stored depth. If z < depth[x,y], write the polygon's colour and set depth[x,y] = z. Otherwise keep the old pixel.

blocks.where: x₁ and x₂ are scan-line endpoints; z₁ and z₂ are their depths; z is the interpolated depth at x.

items: No sorting: polygons may arrive in any order.
Costs one depth array, for example 1920 × 1080 × 4 bytes ≈ 8.3 MB.
Cannot blend transparency through one depth value; polygon edges alias.

blocks.text: A BSP tree is built once for a static scene. Choose one polygon as root. Its plane Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 divides space; A, B, C are the normal components and D fixes the offset. Every other polygon is wholly in front, wholly behind, or crossing. A crossing polygon is split along the plane into two new polygons.

Put front polygons in the front subtree and back polygons in the back subtree; recurse. To display, find which side of each plane holds the eye. Draw the far subtree first, then the root polygon, then the near subtree. This gives back-to-front order without a depth buffer.

BSP build cost and extra polygons are paid once; per-frame sorting is avoided. It suits fixed geometry such as building interiors. Exam questions usually ask for classification and drawing order rather than full BSP construction with polygon splitting.

figure.caption: At pixel (5, 5) the depth starts at 1.0. A at 0.6 passes and is written, then B at 0.4 passes and overwrites it, so the pixel ends with B's colour and depth 0.4. With P1 at x = 2 as the BSP root and the eye at x = 10 in front, the drawing order is P3, P1, P2.

spec.aria: Top: a depth axis from 0 near to 1 far with the start value 1.0, A at 0.6 and B at 0.4, above a three-row trace table of the depth tests. Bottom: planes P3, P1 and P2 at x = 0, 2 and 5 with the eye at x = 10, and the BSP tree with root P1, back child P3 and front child P2, drawn in the order P3, P1, P2.

examples.question: At pixel (5,5), polygon A gives z_A = 0.6 and polygon B gives z_B = 0.4. The depth buffer starts at 1.0; smaller z is nearer. (a) Trace both tests and give the final colour and depth. (b) P1 lies in plane x = 2, P2 at x = 5, P3 at x = 0. Build the BSP tree and give the drawing order for an eye at x = 10.
steps: A: 0.6 < 1.0, so write A's colour, depth = 0.6.
B: 0.4 < 0.6, so overwrite with B's colour, depth = 0.4.
BSP root P1: P3 at x = 0 is back; P2 at x = 5 is front.
Eye at x = 10 is front of P1, so draw back P3, root P1, front P2.
examples.answer: Final pixel: B's colour, depth z = 0.4; BSP drawing order P3, P1, P2.
examples.check:
A=0.6
B=0.4
depth=1.0
if A < depth:
    depth=A
if B < depth:
    depth=B
print(depth)

traps: Using larger z as nearer without stating the convention.
Not resetting the depth buffer to z_far each frame.
Forgetting that a BSP split creates two polygons and changes the count.
Believing the Z-buffer sorts polygons; it tests pixels.
Using one Z-buffer depth for transparent surfaces and expecting correct blending.

quiz.q: What does the depth buffer store?
quiz.a: One depth value per pixel, used to keep the nearest fragment.

quiz.q: Why can painter's algorithm fail on three cyclically overlapping polygons?
quiz.a: No single far-to-near order exists; each polygon is in front of another.

quiz.q: Depth starts at 1.0. Fragments z = 0.8 then z = 0.9 arrive at a pixel. Final depth?
Interpolate z at x = 6 between (x₁ = 2, z₁ = 0.2) and (x₂ = 10, z₂ = 0.6).
Compare Z-buffer and BSP for memory and per-frame sorting.
quiz.a: Z-buffer uses one depth per pixel and no sorting; BSP uses tree memory and splitting, but static scenes draw back to front without per-frame sorting.

quiz.q: BSP root plane x = 3, eye at x = 8; P_back at x = 1, P_front at x = 5. Give order.
quiz.a: Eye is front; draw P_back, root, P_front.

quiz.q: What must happen when a polygon crosses a BSP plane?
quiz.a: Split it into two polygons, one on each side, before inserting.

beyond: Not for the exam. GPUs implement the Z-buffer in hardware and add early-Z tests to reject hidden fragments before shading. Hierarchical Z and depth pre-passes reduce overdraw in dense scenes. BSP trees still appear in static game levels and in constructive solid geometry. Search for depth buffer, early-Z, hierarchical Z, and BSP traversal.
